subject: English
passage:
The following text is adapted from Stephen Crane's 1896 novel George's Mother. George is a young man seeking employment in New York City during the 1890s.

He had entered into an arrangement to work for six months in exchange for a position as clerk in a respectable mercantile establishment, with the understanding that steady employment would follow his period of apprenticeship. [...] When his supervisor dismissed him without cause at the conclusion of his trial period, offering no explanation and refusing to honor the promised permanent position, George—who, though quick-witted and possessed of considerable ambition when circumstances demanded action, had always demonstrated, in his dealings with authority figures, a profound deference and reluctance to assert himself—found himself compelled to seek entirely different prospects for advancement.
prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It indicates that due to a specific trait in his personality, George may have been particularly vulnerable to his employer's unfair treatment.
choices.B: It suggests that George takes pride in a particular aspect of his temperament that he believes distinguishes him from his peers.
choices.C: It demonstrates that George lacks the intellectual capacity and drive needed to succeed in a demanding commercial environment.
choices.D: It clarifies why George is capable of achieving remarkable success when competing against others in challenging situations.

explanation: Choice A is the best answer because the underlined portion indicates that a specific personality trait made George vulnerable to his employer's unfair treatment. The text describes George's dismissal without cause after completing his apprenticeship—his supervisor refused to honor the promised permanent position. The underlined portion reveals that though George was 'quick-witted and possessed of considerable ambition,' he demonstrated 'a profound deference and reluctance to assert himself' with authority figures. This habitual submissiveness to superiors explains why George had no recourse when mistreated and was forced to seek entirely different prospects.
